solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Feature of building computer programs, we hear (4)

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the sound counts, not the spelling

explanation.surface: A remark about software that helps construct buildings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Building computer programs' reads as writing software; 'building' belongs to the definition, and the programs are apps.
explanation.definitionFit: An apse is the rounded recess at the end of a church, an architectural feature.

clue.text: Form of impropriety when academic leads a country (11)

indicators.note: the academic leads, so PROF comes first

explanation.surface: A grumble that it is improper for a professor to become a head of state.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests academics in politics; the word you want is the act of treating something sacred with disrespect.
explanation.definitionFit: Desecrating something sacred is a particular kind of improper behaviour, so the definition names the category.

clue.text: Poet’s village festival entertaining a hundred folk regularly (4,5)

indicators.note: a host entertaining guests holds them, so EASTER goes round the rest
take letters at regular intervals: every other one

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of f-O-l-K

explanation.surface: A village festival in a poem, with a crowd of a hundred or so turning up.
explanation.walkthrough: East Coker is a Somerset village, and the title of one of T. S. Eliot's Four Quartets; 'Poet's village' is the one Eliot wrote about and where his ashes lie.
explanation.definitionFit: East Coker is the village T. S. Eliot named a poem after and is buried in.

clue.text: Good humour always at home in the course of game (10)

indicators.note: during the game, so EER and IN go inside CHESS

blocks.note: chess is a game, split around the rest

explanation.surface: Someone who stays cheerful whenever there is a home game on.
explanation.walkthrough: EER is the old poetic form of ever, a crossword staple for 'always'.
explanation.definitionFit: Cheeriness is a cheerful, good-humoured disposition.

clue.text: King, say, upset, being taken in by bounders and scroungers (7)

indicators.note: upset in a down clue turns the letters upward, reversing them
the reversed letters are taken inside CADS

blocks.note: a cad or bounder is a dishonourable man

explanation.surface: A monarch is knocked over and swallowed up by a gang of rogues and spongers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'King, say' looks like one idea, a king as an example; it is two pieces, R and EG, which together make REG before being upset.
explanation.definitionFit: Cadgers are people who scrounge things from others.

clue.text: Momentous things are threat somehow (5-10)

indicators.note: arranged in some way or other, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A worried claim that momentous events are somehow menacing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Momentous things' reads as a noun phrase; the definition is only 'Momentous', and 'things' starts the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something earth-shattering is momentous, of huge importance.

clue.text: Flighty type narrated story in auditorium (7)

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so the sound counts

explanation.surface: A fickle performer told a story on stage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flighty type' suggests a capricious person; it means something that flies, the red-tailed hawk.
explanation.definitionFit: A redtail is a red-tailed hawk, a bird and so a flying type.

clue.text: Old priest with the heartless description of the chosen people (5)

indicators.note: without its heart, the middle letter of THE goes

blocks.note: Eli is the Old Testament priest who raised Samuel

explanation.surface: An Old Testament priest describing the Israelites as God's chosen people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The chosen people' suggests the Biblical Israelites, in keeping with Eli; here it is simply a select few.
explanation.definitionFit: The elite are the select group, those picked out as the best.

clue.text: Barely sufficient examination taking minimal time (5)

indicators.note: the least of the word, just its first letter

blocks.note: a scan is a medical examination

explanation.surface: An exam so rushed it barely counts.
explanation.walkthrough: T is also the standard abbreviation for time.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means barely enough, scarcely sufficient.

clue.text: Looked at team showing anger maybe after trick (10)

indicators.note: team and anger come after the trick, so CON goes first

blocks.note: red is the colour of anger, as in seeing red

explanation.surface: A referee eyes a team losing their temper after someone is fooled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags anger as an example of what RED can stand for.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the thinking sense: a matter you have looked at is one you have weighed up.

clue.text: Capital this person’s invested in American city (4)

indicators.note: money invested in something is put into it, so I goes inside LA

blocks.note: this person is = the speaker saying I am, contracted to I'M

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of having capital invested in an American city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Capital' sounds like money to invest; it is a capital city. 'This person's' is the setter speaking of themself: this person is = I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Peru's seat of government is one capital city among many.

clue.text: Left in Calais, unable to communicate successfully? (6)

blocks.note: Calais is in France, so the French word for left

explanation.surface: A traveller stranded in France who cannot make themself understood.
explanation.walkthrough: Calais is the French port, so 'in Calais' asks for the French word; the question mark admits the second definition is loose, since gauche means socially clumsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Gauche is French for left, and in English means awkward and tactless in company.

clue.text: Competes in race that’s most laborious (8)

indicators.note: competitors are in a race, taking part inside it, so VIES sits inside HEAT

blocks.note: a heat is a qualifying race

explanation.surface: An athlete running in the toughest race of the meeting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Competes in race' reads as a single action; it is the instruction to put one word inside the other, with 'that's' linking to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Heavy has a sense of hard and tiring, as in heavy going, so the superlative matches 'most laborious'.

clue.text: Unexpected gains with politicians — those endorsing proposal? (11)

indicators.note: an unexpected form of the word is a rearranged one

blocks.note: Tories are members of the British Conservative Party

explanation.surface: Surprise election gains for a party whose members back a policy.
explanation.walkthrough: Tories are the British Conservatives; the question mark concedes that signatories sign a document rather than a proposal as such.
explanation.definitionFit: Signatories are those who put their names to an agreement, endorsing it.

clue.text: Pitch made by one favouring war? (4)

blocks.note: the verb: to pitch goods, peddling them in the street
the political term for an aggressive advocate of military action, opposite of a dove

explanation.surface: A speech or sales pitch delivered by a warmonger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pitch made by' reads as a noun; the first definition is the verb, to pitch wares, and 'made by' joins it to the second.
explanation.definitionFit: Hawking is peddling goods by pitching them, and a hawk is a political advocate of war.

clue.text: What’s carried by ship is scary — discarded loot (10)

indicators.note: cargo carried by a ship is inside it, so the ship's letters go round the next word

explanation.surface: A frightening pirate ship whose cargo is abandoned plunder.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Loot' is slang for money; the schilling was Austria's currency, discarded when the euro arrived.
explanation.definitionFit: Schillings were Austrian money, replaced by the euro in 2002, so cash that has been discarded.

clue.text: A three-legged race location (4,2,3)

blocks.note: the surface reads a sports-day race with pairs tied together; the setter means a race held somewhere whose emblem has three legs, the TT motorcycle races
the place itself: an island in the Irish Sea whose flag shows three armoured legs

explanation.surface: Where the school sports-day three-legged race is being held.
explanation.walkthrough: A three-legged race is a sports-day event with pairs tied together; here 'three-legged' describes the place, whose flag bears three legs, and the race is the TT.
explanation.definitionFit: The Isle of Man's symbol is the triskelion of three armoured legs, and its TT races are famous.

clue.text: Small unit that could make mice tremor (10)

indicators.note: the letters could be made into something else

explanation.surface: A tiny measure fine enough to register mice trembling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tremor' suggests measuring vibration, which suits a small unit; it is only fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A micrometre is a millionth of a metre, a small unit of length.

clue.text: Greek character leading board not necessarily permanent (7)

indicators.note: the Greek letter goes in front

blocks.note: mu is the twelfth Greek letter
a board is a table, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A Greek chairing a board whose membership keeps changing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Greek character leading board' sounds like a person in charge; the character is a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by negation: liable to change is the opposite of fixed, so 'not necessarily permanent' says the same thing.

clue.text: Identity needed to enter sporting occasion? That is obvious (7)

indicators.note: ID has to enter the event, going inside it

explanation.surface: A steward says it is plain that you need identification to get into the match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is obvious' reads as a comment; the definition is only 'obvious'.
explanation.definitionFit: Evident means plain to see, obvious.

clue.text: Irishman bringing post around (4)

indicators.note: turned around, so the letters run backwards

explanation.surface: An Irish postman doing the rounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Around' looks like the postman's rounds; it turns the word back to front.
explanation.definitionFit: Liam is an Irish man's name, the Irish form of William.

clue.text: One drafted in — being cute, I end getting redeployed (8)

indicators.note: the letters are deployed again in a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A conscript complains that looking sweet gets them posted somewhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drafted' and 'redeployed' both sound military, which suits an inductee, a conscript enrolled in the forces.
explanation.definitionFit: An inductee is someone formally enlisted, drafted in to the armed forces.

clue.text: African country set up to accommodate second religion (5)

indicators.note: set up in a down clue raises the letters, reversing them
MALI accommodates S, holding it inside

explanation.surface: An African nation is organised so as to make room for a second faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'African country' could be the definition, but only 'religion' fits five letters; MALI read upward gives ILAM, which takes S after its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the faith of Muslims is one of the world's major religions.

clue.text: Part of ship storing bit of rotten rubbish (5)

indicators.note: the deck stores the letter inside it
just a bit of the word, its first letter

blocks.note: a deck is part of a ship

explanation.surface: A ship's hold full of putrid refuse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten rubbish' reads as one phrase; 'rotten' only supplies R, and 'rubbish' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Dreck, from Yiddish, means trash or rubbish.

clue.text: Figure is round and not totally lifeless (6)

indicators.note: not the whole word, so its last letter goes

blocks.note: GONE = dead, minus its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone describes a shape that is round and barely alive.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Figure is round' suggests a circle; an isogon is a polygon with all angles equal.
explanation.definitionFit: An isogon is a geometric figure whose angles are all equal.

clue.text: Meeting female, give false account willingly (4)

indicators.note: the female meets the lie, joining it end to end

blocks.note: to lie is to give a false account

explanation.surface: On meeting a woman, someone readily tells lies.
explanation.walkthrough: Lief is archaic, surviving in 'I would as lief', meaning I would as gladly.
explanation.definitionFit: Lief is an old word meaning gladly or willingly.

clue.text: British journeys frenetic, needing introduction of one female attendant (10)

indicators.note: I is introduced into MAD, going inside

explanation.surface: A harried British commute that could use someone to help out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'British' gives only B, not BR, so RIDES follows at once.
explanation.definitionFit: A bridesmaid is a woman attending the bride at a wedding.

clue.text: Insignificant person to enforce delay upon being picked up (10)

indicators.note: picked up by the ear, so the sound counts

blocks.note: to make someone wait is to enforce a delay

explanation.surface: A petty official who makes people wait just because they can.
explanation.walkthrough: A makeweight is something added to make up a weight, so a person there only to fill numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: A makeweight is a person or thing of little value included only to make up the numbers.

clue.text: Numbers given hotel grub (4)

blocks.note: H = hotel in the phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Hotel guests are given room numbers and fed.
explanation.walkthrough: Nosh and grub are both British slang for food.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosh is informal British slang for food, just like grub.
